runs.text: Price elasticity of supply is percentage quantity-supplied change divided by percentage price change. The midpoint method divides each change by the average of its starting and ending values. Elasticity above one means a more-than-proportional quantity response. Spare capacity, storage, and time to adjust production generally make supply more elastic.

transcript.sourceText: The price rises from $4 to $8. On the short-run curve, quantity rises from 60 to 70, so the midpoint quantity change is 10/65 = 15.4%; the midpoint price change is 4/6 = 66.7%. Short-run supply elasticity is 15.4%/66.7% = 0.23, which is inelastic. The flatter long-run curve shows a larger quantity response.
transcript.text: The price rises from 4 dollars to 8 dollars . On the short-run curve, quantity rises from 60 to 70, so the midpoint quantity change is 10 divided by 65 equals 15.4 percent ; the midpoint price change is 4 divided by 6 equals 66.7 percent . Short-run supply elasticity is 15.4 percent divided by 66.7 percent equals 0.23 , which is inelastic. The flatter long-run curve shows a larger quantity response.

MICROECONOMICS

Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Measure Price Elasticity of Supply.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Price elasticity of supply is percentage quantity-supplied change divided by percentage price change. The midpoint method divides each change by the average of its starting and ending values. Elasticity above one means a more-than-proportional quantity response. Spare capacity, storage, and time to adjust production generally make supply more elastic.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a percentage change in quantity supplied caused by a percentage change in the good's price.
Compute elasticity as percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.
A larger elasticity means sellers respond more strongly to the price change.
Supply is usually more elastic when firms have more time or spare capacity to adjust production.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse supply elasticity with demand shifters. Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHORT-RUN VERSUS LONG-RUN SUPPLY

The price rises from $4 to $8. On the short-run curve, quantity rises from 60 to 70, so the midpoint quantity change is 10/65 = 15.4%; the midpoint price change is 4/6 = 66.7%. Short-run supply elasticity is 15.4%/66.7% = 0.23, which is inelastic. The flatter long-run curve shows a larger quantity response.
